newsitem.title: ITALY: FEATURE - Naples crib makers feel pinch as Italians cut back.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Naples crib makers feel pinch as Italians cut back.

text.p: Italians, counting the cost of Christmas with the prospect of a big "Euro-tax" in the new year, are cutting back on one of their favourite seasonal adornments -- the nativity crib.
Shoppers traditionally flock to a tiny cobbled street in the ancient heart of Naples to buy elaborate sructures styled from cork and wood and meticulously crafted figures to go in them.

This year, as Italians prepare for the pain of a special tax designed to help them qualify to join a single European currency, there is more room to stroll and browse in the capital of crib making, the street of San Gregorio Armeno.
"Last year you couldn't move on this street from December 1," said one woman studying all the figurines on display in one shop, but without buying. "It's different this year."
SALES DROP 40 PERCENT

"This year, we're seeing a crisis in Italy because we're being buried in taxes," said Giuseppe Ferrigno, a veteran artisan whose family has had a bustling workshop in San Gregorio Armeno turning out "pastori", or crib figurines, since 1836.
"People are afraid to spend money. There's inflation and now this Euro-tax. Sales are 40 percent less than last year."

Giuseppe Cesarini, one of only a handful of artisans to make truly traditional crib figures with terracotta heads, arms and feet fixed to flexible body frames of metal bound with string, said people were still buying but were far more cautious.
Traditional pastori can cost one million lire ($650) or more each, depending on size and quality.
"It's tougher compared to other years," Cesarini said. "There's this war of taxes. People are weighing their lire more, they're not rushing in and buying on impulse."
Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left government has drawn up a tough budget for 1997 to try to ensure Italy does not get left behind as Europe pushes on to economic union.
It contains unpopular tax hikes and the one-off Euro-levy, due to be paid early next year. Italians are still waiting for details of how the new tax will hit them.
LABOUR OF LOVE

Cesarini, a master sculptor by trade, will cheerfully admit that he "can't live off pastori all year round". His workshop contains a near life-sized statue of a Madonna which he is restoring -- the kind of job that is his bread and butter.
But he says the crib work is another artistic satisfaction. He smiles indulgently and gives in when a well-dressed man haggles to reduce the price of a crib contained in a bell-jar.

Ferrigno, a talkative Neapolitan who began making figurines 56 years ago at the age of five, says the success of his family firm means he could give up work. But he cannot tear himself away from what he calls a labour of love.
Though sales are down, his creations are much sought after. One woman bought two costly figurines at once -- keeping trade ticking over nicely.
To another shopper, lingering over pricey Madonnas dressed in cloth and other traditional figures, he simply shrugged and said quality doesn't come cheap.
CUSTOM OR KITSCH?
Neapolitans say they gave birth to the crib tradition centuries ago and that the golden age was in the 1700s under King Carlos III of Spain, who ruled the southern port city.

Rich merchants followed the royal vogue for elaborate porcelain scenes which gradually moved away from the nativity to become mini-representations of themes and characters from the emerging popular theatre.
"That was the most beautiful age of the cribs," said Cesarini, who works from reproductions to try to make exact copies of the traditional figures for modern homes.
Today, cribs can be large, elaborate affairs a bit like dolls' houses -- complete with street scenes, steps, lights and waterfalls, that have little or nothing to do with Christmas.
Pastori makers have also moved with the times.

Angelo Lofredo's stall at the start of the street grabs the attention of passers-by with its figurines of protagonists in the sweeping corruption investigations which have transformed Italy's political landscape since 1992.

Former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi, now on trial in two separate corruption probes, was a hot seller two years ago and the crusading anti-graft magistrate Antonio Di Pietro was shown as a hero with a halo of flashing lights.
The hugely popular Di Pietro has since quit as both a magistrate and a minister and was placed under investigation himself last month.
Ferrigno, who joins in the fun with a few novelty creations each year, gave Di Pietro a taste of his own medicine by showing him as a downcast figure banging on the bars of a prison cell.
For Italians really fed up with their turbulent politics, he had also made a small scene, painted scarlet, showing politicians as devils amid the flames.
"They're in hell because they're the ones who have crucified Italy," Ferrigno said.
